title: The far right’s win in Germany is sending a chill through the establishment in Europe
description: Alternative for Germany (AfD) may not have won the supermajority it sought in the Saxony-Anhalt state election on Sunday, but the far-right party did take another giant step toward power in a country ...
fullText:
Alternative for Germany (AfD) may not have won the supermajority it sought in the Saxony-Anhalt state election on Sunday, but the far-right party did take another giant step toward power in a country whose postwar democracy was designed to prevent the return of right-wing extremism. The AfD's win, which co-leader Alice Weidel described as "historic," also showed that in Germany, as elsewhere in Europe, the center is not holding as firmly as it once did.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said the AfD's victory has shaken his conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) "to its very foundations" and would have "consequences" reaching well beyond the region.

"It is an election result we cannot simply move past as if nothing happened," he said Monday. "It is the most severe election defeat the CDU has suffered in years, indeed in decades."

On Sunday, the CDU didn't just lose support to the AfD at the margins, but more than half its 2021 vote outright, with the AfD more than doubling its own share in the former East German state to 44% in a single electoral cycle.

The AfD was already the largest opposition party in the federal parliament in Berlin, making the "eastern exception" argument — that this is a regional, post-Communist phenomenon — harder to sustain. The CDU's rhetoric on migration has shifted further right as the AFD's popularity has grown. And with each win at state level, the "Brandmauer," or "firewall against the far-right," that prevents ultra-nationalist parties like AfD from joining ruling coalitions is being tested a little more by parliamentary arithmetic as much as by principle. The question now is: How much longer can a democratic argument be made to justify the firewall?

A similar question is also facing Europe as a whole. In Brussels, the so-called "cordon sanitaire," the European Union's own version of the far-right firewall, is also under pressure from mathematics.

Three hard-right groups hold 196 seats combined in the European Parliament, representing parties from more than a dozen member states. Together, they represent the Parliament's second-largest force by seat count, even though the three rarely vote as a bloc. And while they remain walled off from the EU's top jobs, they are already reshaping the organization's debates on migration, aid to Ukraine and the "Green Deal" aimed at reaching climate neutrality.

At national level, too, far-right parties now lead coalitions in Italy and the Czech Republic and serve as junior governing partners in Finland, Croatia, Slovakia and Sweden. And where the far right doesn't hold power, it is still setting the terms of the debate: The Freedom Party of Austria (FPÖ) topped Austria's national vote in 2024, Geert Wilders' Party for Freedom (PVV) remains one of the largest blocs in the Dutch parliament despite the collapse of its coalition last year, and Marine Le Pen's National Rally has been France's most consistently popular party for years. In Italy, Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has spent four years proving a party with post-fascist roots can govern from the center-right without spooking financial markets.

Hungary's election in April showed that the far right's advance is not purely linear: Péter Magyar's center-right Tisza party ousted Viktor Orbán's illiberal Fidesz party in a landslide, ending 16 years of authoritarian rule and proving that entrenched incumbents can still lose.

But the far right doesn't need to win everywhere, every time; it has already changed what Europe's mainstream parties have to contend with and campaign against.

The historic mainstream now also faces increasing pressure from abroad. No longer just from Moscow, but also from Washington and MAGA, too. Elon Musk endorsed the AfD ahead of last year's federal election, appearing at a campaign rally to declare it would "save the future of civilization." US Vice President JD Vance used his 2025 Munich Security Conference speech to attack Germany's far-right firewall directly and met with Weidel days before the vote.

One senior German politician at the time called Vance's support "a big boost to the far right in Germany and in Europe." AfD figures campaign on the idea of establishing good relations with both the White House and the Kremlin, as Saxony-Anhalt's own AfD candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, did in the run-up to Sunday's vote.

None of which should distract from the very real home-grown popularity of far-right parties in Europe, which is rooted in domestic grievances over immigration, stagnant wages, deindustrialization and the failure of mainstream parties to address that discontent. What it does mean, though, is that Europe's far right isn't simply rising on its own. Rather, it is being actively reinforced by outside powers that have their own reasons — ideological and geostrategic — to want Europe's postwar center to fracture.

The question now is just how unstoppable the far right's rise in Europe really is. The answer should come into sharper focus over the next 18 months, as France heads toward a 2027 presidential race. Le Pen, the far-right leader, now appears to be the favorite in opinion polls.

In the shorter term, voters in Berlin and Mecklenburg, in northeastern Germany, head to the polls in under two weeks. Those local elections could show whether Sunday's result in Saxony-Anhalt represents a ceiling for the far right's rise in Europe — or just its latest floor.

title: All 5 killed in Miami cargo jet crash were in a van used by plane cleaners
description: The five people killed when an Amazon cargo jet ran off the runway at Miami International Airport were all inside a van used to shuttle crews that clean planes, authorities said.  The pilot and co-pil...
fullText:
MIAMI (AP) — The five people killed when an Amazon cargo jet ran off the runway at Miami International Airport were all inside a van used to shuttle crews that clean planes, authorities said.

The jet overran the runway while landing Sunday. It slammed into the van on airport property, careened through a fence and then smashed an SUV on a city street.

Five other people were injured. The pilot and co-pilot have been released from the hospital, Miami-Dade County Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz said Tuesday. Two people remain in critical condition, while a third is in stable condition, she said.

The National Transportation Safety Board is investigating the crash. One focus will be on the lack of a system to slow and stop speeding jets at the end of runways.

Miami is not one of the 120 airports in the U.S. with lightweight, crushable material that the Federal Aviation Administration says has saved around 500 lives.

Even without a runway excursion system, Miami's airport appears to be compliant with federal rules because it has a 1,000-foot (305-meter) safety buffer at the end of its runways, experts said.

NTSB Chairwoman Jennifer Homendy said her agency's goal is to prevent tragedies, but runway excursions continue to happen even after the board has suggested installing the systems in the past.

"Our recommendations must be implemented or we're going to be here again," she said at a Monday news conference.

Investigators recovered the flight data recorder and the information is being reviewed. Interviews with the pilot, co-pilot, air traffic controllers and others are being scheduled, Homendy said.

Amazon said in a statement that it is cooperating with the investigation and the company's deepest sympathies go to the victims and their families.

The five people killed were all in a van owned by Professional Ocean Service Corp., a company that cleans planes. The company said it wouldn't comment on the crash out of respect for the families who lost loved ones.

"Our employees are far more than the people who work beside us each day, they are family, and they are deeply loved. Our hearts and prayers are with every employee and every family whose lives have been forever changed," the company said in a statement Tuesday.

The Miami-Dade sheriff identified the deceased as Rolando Aleman Leon, 55; Yoel Rodriguez Naranjo, 53; Julio C. Pineda, 75; Carlos Acosta Fajardo, 53; and Javierkys Reyes Quevedo, 47.

The Amazon jet was landing after a two-hour flight from Puerto Rico as storms brewed around the Miami airport.

The NTSB said the plane barreled roughly 1,300 feet (396 meters) past the end of the runway.

Homendy called the scene "utter devastation," with pieces of the vehicles, air bags, destroyed navigational equipment and fencing along the plane's route. She said she had to be careful because jet fuel was still all around 24 hours after the crash.

Strong winds over 25 knots were reported Saturday afternoon. Experts who viewed video of the landing said it appears that a strong tail wind propelled the plane far down the runway past the point where it was supposed to land. The plane remained airborne without flaring the nose to force the wheels onto the ground.

It is not immediately clear why the pilot didn't abort landing and go around to try again.

Air traffic controllers also had not changed the approach to the runway to allow the plane to land into a headwind. Airports routinely change which direction planes land on a runway when the winds shift.

The flight had been operated by 21 Air, a cargo carrier based in North Carolina. The 32-year-old Boeing 767 was originally built to carry passengers and flew for several airlines in foreign countries for more than two decades before being converted to a cargo plane in 2015, according to flight-tracking site Flightradar24.

Two of the four runways at the Miami airport remained closed Tuesday, and Homendy said they will not be reopened until NTSB investigators gather all the information they need from the crash scene.

More than 225 flights were canceled Sunday and Monday, and hundreds more were delayed, officials said.

Homendy said the NTSB will try to release the runway back to the airport as quickly as possible after investigators document the scene.

Funk reported from Omaha, Nebraska, and Collins reported from Columbia, South Carolina.

Due to an error in a news release from the Miami-Dade County Sheriff's Office, an earlier version of this story misspelled the last name of victim Yoel Rodriguez Naranjo.

title: Calls to halt cycle bridge plan in Roman village
description: Plans to add a cycle lane to Dilston Bridge meet resistance from some Corbridge villagers.
fullText:
Residents of a hamlet that dates back to Roman times are calling for plans to install a cycle lane on their Grade-II listed bridge to be halted.

Northumberland County Council is to reduce the two-lane traffic flow on Dilston Bridge in Corbridge to a single lane, install traffic lights either side and use the newly-created space for the cycle path.

Some locals say the plans risk "urbanising" and "changing the character" of the village and cause congestion by creating a traffic bottleneck.

Campaigners want a heritage consultation over the plan, but the council said it was not required and the bridge itself was not being altered or demolished.

The bridge plan is part of a wider saga around a project to create a walking and cycling route between Hexham and Corbridge, which was approved in 2023 and is being paid for for by the then-government's Levelling Up Fund.

The council said it will "improve access to employment, education and transport hubs while supporting healthier, more sustainable travel choices".

Campaigner David Burdus, who has lived in Corbridge for 25 years, said objectors were not against active travel and he welcomed improved accessibility, particularly as he uses a powered wheelchair.

But he said: "We're not supportive of particular points along the route being historically destroyed.

"We're going to turn a free flow of movement into a stop, start, stop, start.

"It's going to cause havoc, pollution, and disturbance.

"This area is a visitor attraction and it relies on tourism and you're going to turn this beautiful hamlet into a road traffic bottleneck. There's no need."

He argued the number of listed buildings in the area, close to Hadrian's Wall, meant a heritage consultation should have been carried out and the council needed listed building consent.

The council said listed building status did not extend to the "character or setting" of a structure and it considered the active travel scheme to fall under Permitted Development rules laid out by the government.

It said it was required by government to prioritise active travel to improve public health and reduce pollution.

title: Ukraine prosecutor general resigns in latest fallout from anti-corruption crackdown
description: KYIV, Sept 8 (Reuters) - Ukraine's prosecutor general resigned his post late on Monday after a corruption investigation reached his office, becoming the latest senior official ensnared in an ‌intensif...
fullText:
KYIV, Sept 8 (Reuters) - Ukraine's prosecutor general resigned his post late on Monday after a corruption investigation reached his office, becoming the latest senior official ensnared in an ‌intensified anti-graft crackdown by Kyiv's independent watchdogs.

Ruslan Kravchenko was not charged with a crime or named ‌a suspect in any investigation. But authorities had accused a subordinate of helping run a fraud ring, prompting the presidential appointee to ​quit to avoid "political confrontation".

"This is a political decision, and I have made it consciously," said Kravchenko, 36, in a statement. He denied any wrongdoing.

The case is the latest in a series of high-profile corruption scandals that have claimed the jobs of senior officials in President Volodymyr Zelenskiy's government and forced several wartime shake-ups.

Zelenskiy said on Tuesday he ‌would submit Kravchenko's request to parliament, ⁠where lawmakers must approve his resignation.

The investigation by the NABU and SAPO agencies, announced on Saturday, centres on a department manager whom prosecutors say took bribes ⁠for helping to cover up a call centre that defrauded Ukrainians and foreigners.

They said the official recruited fellow employees and friends to launder nearly $1 million in proceeds through real estate purchases and other assets.

The agencies published photos of a ​safe ​filled with stacks of cash and detectives confiscating a luxury ​SUV.

Such vivid instances of alleged graft have ‌fuelled public anger at a time when Ukraine is fighting for survival against Russia.

Last year, Zelenskiy faced the worst political crisis of the war after his ex-business partner was accused of running a $100 million kickback scheme at the state atomic agency.

CALLS TO REFORM PROSECUTOR'S OFFICE

Kravchenko had been criticised by opponents for allegedly participating in an attempt to roll back the powers of NABU and SAPO last year - accusations he has denied.

In Ukraine, the ‌prosecutor's office enjoys considerable powers, ranging from probing corruption to ​investigating war crimes.

Zelenskiy, who had faced protests last year over ​the proposed restrictions on the anti-corruption agencies, said ​on Tuesday that he had met with Kravchenko as well as NABU and SAPO ‌following the latest investigation.

Opposition lawmaker Andrii Osadchuk, deputy ​chair of parliament's law-enforcement committee, ​said the scandal underlines the need to reform the prosecution service and called for key posts to be filled through open competition.

Fighting corruption is also critical to Kyiv's bid for membership in ​the European Union.

"It will be very ‌difficult for Ukraine to move forward if we do not change the approach to selecting and ​appointing the prosecutor general and prosecutors at lower levels," Osadchuk said.

(Additional reporting by Jekaterīna Golubkova ​in Tokyo; Editing by Stephen Coates and Ros Russell)

title: Ex-Penn State assistant football coach Jerry Sandusky withdraws petition for new sex abuse trial in state court
description: Former Penn State assistant football coach Jerry Sandusky withdrew his petition for a new trial at a hearing Tuesday morning with plans to pursue federal relief, according to a spokesperson for Sandusky.
fullText:
Former Penn State assistant football coach Jerry Sandusky withdrew his petition for a new trial at a hearing Tuesday morning with plans to pursue federal relief, according to a spokesperson for Sandusky.

A judge in Centre County, Pennsylvania, accepted the withdrawal of Sandusky's petition at the state court hearing.

Sandusky, who was convicted of sex abuse in 2012, appeared virtually from prison to officially tell the court he'd like to withdraw the petition, filed last year.

Attorneys for Sandusky notified the court last week of his intentions but the judge kept Tuesday's hearing on the schedule so she could hear from the disgraced football coach about the reversal.

A victim who testified against Sandusky in his original trial was scheduled to publicly recant his allegations in court on Tuesday at what was set to be an evidentiary hearing.

Sandusky has always maintained he is innocent and, according to the spokesperson, opted to withdraw his efforts in state court to pursue what he hopes to be a faster appellate route in federal court.

Lawyers for Sandusky have fought his conviction for more than a decade and now at his age, time is of the essence.

"I need to get there as fast as possible. I'm 82 years old. I'm innocent. I intend to be alive when the truth is heard," Sandusky said in an audio statement from prison shared with CNN last week.

Sandusky's legal team filed the latest post-conviction relief petition for a new trial last year based on several issues. A judge batted down most of the arguments but did grant the evidentiary hearing based on the recantation from a man who testified at Sandusky's trial as Alleged Victim No. 10.

"I now regret my role in facilitating what I have come to view as a deeply flawed prosecution," wrote Ryan Rittmeyer, known in the trial as Alleged Victim No. 10, in a 2025 affidavit. Rittmeyer is the only victim of Sandusky who has recanted, and he is connected to only six of the 45 counts against the coach.

Sandusky will not be able to pursue federal relief based on the recantation because the petition was not exhausted in state court. With his lawyers, Sandusky now intends to file a petition in federal court to continue fighting his conviction based on other issues that were unsuccessful in previous state appeals.

"Over the years, I have brought 15 serious issues before Pennsylvania's courts, each one showing I deserve a new trial. Everyone was swatted down," Sandusky said in the recorded statement. "I have no faith this one would be treated differently, no matter how compelling the evidence in federal court, every one of those issues can be heard together by judges who have not already made up their minds about me."

The coach, who called himself the "Great Pretender," was sentenced to 30 to 60 years in 2012 for sexually abusing 10 boys over a 15-year period. Many of them were connected to The Second Mile, a charity Sandusky started in 1977 as a group foster home, which had grown to encompass a broad range of programs for disadvantaged young people.

At the trial, victims described in detail multiple instances of oral sex when they were teenagers – sometimes in a basement, sometimes in a shower.

This story has been updated with additional information.

title: Newsom admits democratic socialist ideas ‘mainstream’ in Democrat party: ‘Pretty aligned’
description: California Gov. Gavin Newsom says the Democratic Party is "pretty aligned" with the DSA on Medicare for All, climate change and fossil fuels.
fullText:
In an interview discussing his rumored 2028 presidential run, California Gov. Gavin Newsom asserted that the Democratic Party is "pretty aligned" with the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), especially when it comes to universal healthcare, climate change and moving away from fossil fuel usage.

During an interview with "PBS NewsHour," Newsom was questioned about what recent democratic socialist victories across the country mean for the Democratic Party.

"If you have these candidates and this platform that is clearly animating the base, energizing turnout, should more of those ideas be worked into the broader Democratic platform?" Newsom was asked.

"I think they are," Newsom shot back. "I mean, we want money out of politics. I've been supporting clean money campaigns for decades."

Newsom Tells Democrats To Be In The 'Addition Not Subtraction' Business With Socialists

The interviewer pressed Newsom further, saying, "There seems to be some distance between [Democratic] leadership and those DSA candidates."

"But, not the ideas," Newsom responded.

"I believe in universal healthcare, and I believe in Medicare for All, the party does overwhelmingly," he said. "And so, if it's about more money in your pocket, lowering costs, getting money out of politics, if it's about Medicare for All, I think we're pretty aligned."

He added, "It's about recognizing that we've got a planet that is getting hotter and drier and that we've got to address the issue of climate change, we want energy security, and we want to move off fossil fuels. That's a DSA position, that's a mainstream position within the Democratic Party."

Newsom dismissed worry about democratic socialist influence in American politics, saying, "I think in many ways, it's just a label … it's just such a familiar label to me, we call them progressives."

Newsom Hit With Lawsuit Threat As Whistleblower Begs Trump For Help With 'Monumental' Fraud Scandal

"Maybe it's just because I'm from California and I think it's healthy … I'm not consumed by this," the governor continued, adding that the DSA's ideas reflect "aspects and component parts of our party that we've always had, and it's a healthy dialectic within the party."

Fox News Digital reached out to Newsom's office for additional comment. Fox News Digital also reached out to the DSA and to the Democratic National Committee for comment.

The DSA is the pre-eminent socialist political group in the U.S. This year, the group rolled out an updated platform that includes eliminating the Senate and replacing the president and the Supreme Court with an executive and judiciary chosen by Congress. Additionally, the updated platform includes amnesty for all immigrants and defunding the Department of War.

Jennifer Siebel Newsom Dodges Question On Husband Gavin's Presidential Aspirations

This is in addition to the DSA's already existing policy platform, which calls for an "immediate end to all deportations," free migration between countries without restrictive immigration controls, and "extending full voting rights to people with criminal convictions and noncitizens."

Once considered a fringe movement on the Democratic Party's progressive wing, the DSA has been gaining relevance, with several of its members toppling longtime establishment party figures. This has prompted many to speculate that the DSA represents the Democratic Party's future.

title: The world now has more people aged 65 and over than children under 5—but America is actually getting younger relative to the rest of the globe
description: The Census Bureau found that in 2025, the United States ranked as the 48th-oldest country out of 227 countries. By 2060, the U.S. will fall to 110th place as other regions age more rapidly.
fullText:
Population levels across the world have reached a tipping point: The U.S. Census Bureau reported that in 2025, for the first time in human history, the share of adults age 65 and over outnumbered the share of children aged 5 and under. 

Declining birth rates and an aging population present unique problems for individuals and governments: For individuals, it comes down to financing a longer life and potentially moving milestones as a result. For policymakers, it means budgeting services over a longer period, with demand levels increasing in the coming decades.

But despite policymakers and private-market voices raising the alarm over U.S. demographics, the U.S. will actually become relatively younger than the rest of the world over the next few decades.

The Census Bureau, in a report published last week, found that in 2025, the United States ranked as the 48th-oldest country out of 227 countries. By 2060, the U.S. will fall to 110th place because other regions are aging more rapidly.

In 2025, Japan had the world's oldest population, with 29.7% aged 65 and older. This was followed by Germany and Greece, at approximately 25%.

However, come 2060, Japan will drop to the third-oldest country, with South Korea projected to see 41% of its population above the age of 65. This will be followed by Taiwan at approximately 40%.

While Europe is expected to remain the world's oldest region (the percent of its population aged 65 and over is projected to increase from 21.% to 30.8% between 2025 and 2060), the report adds that in the same period, 160 countries—mostly in Africa, Asia, Latin America, and the Caribbean—have populations aged 85 and over which are expected to quadruple.

However, just because U.S. policymakers won't have to adjust to population shifts as rapidly as other nations, that doesn't mean it won't have to wrangle with associated macroeconomic factors—budgeting and productivity, for example.

BlackRock CEO Larry Fink, for example, has suggested that America could rethink its retirement age to preserve programs like Social Security for younger generations. Moreover, if people could be broadly expected to work a year or so longer, then the labor force would be relatively larger than expected—and therefore produce more during that period.

Yet for the U.S. in particular, there's a problem. Just because people are living longer doesn't mean they're necessarily getting more "healthy" years—years which could be spent more comfortably continuing to work.

The Census Bureau reports that in the U.S., the proportion of years lived in full health after the age of 60 has actually decreased, down 2 percentage points between 2000 and 2019. That figure was slightly higher for men than for women.

The report also highlights that between 2016 and 2019, 73% of adults over the age of 65 lived with two or more chronic health issues, and were more likely to have mobility issues earlier on. In 2018, for example, around 60% of U.S. adults reported mobility problems, compared with 30% of the same age group living in Switzerland.

Macroeconomic shifts arising from an older population are already evident in the U.S. economy. Jobs in health and social care have been a key driver of employment growth over the past 12 months, adding an average of 32,000 roles per month.

This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

title: Ukrainian woman designing a ballistic missile to put Moscow in reach
description: Before Russia invaded, Iryna Terekh designed patios. Now she runs a Ukrainian defense company testing a missile she says will soon put Moscow in range.
fullText:
Kyiv — Ukraine's most important weapons manufacturer wears mismatched earrings and a black knit dress.

"The good thing about being the boss is that you get to set the dress code," Iryna Terekh, the 34-year-old CEO of Fire Point, one of Ukraine's largest drone makers, told CBS News, grinning as she took a seat next to a model of one of the company's latest designs.

With her high heels, bright smile, and entourage of millennial assistants and executives, Terekh stands out in her factory, where throngs of middle-aged men lug drone parts, wield power tools and chain-smoke cigarettes. But she is hardly an exception in a country forced to reinvent itself since Russia launched its invasion in February 2022.

"When the full-scale invasion started, a lot of people had to review what could be their personal impact," she said. "You never really know what kind of knowledge and what kind of experience could be transformed and pivoted into something new."

Terekh's experience was in design and management.

Trained as an architect in the northern Ukrainian city of Irpin, she started building patios and outdoor furniture while also developing a successful high-performance concrete company.

In the early months of 2022, Russian forces occupied Irpin, destroying roughly 70% of the city.

"I understood how vulnerable we are to the complete barbarian behavior of our enemy," Terekh told CBS News. "And if there are any competences that I could put on the table for the sake of fighting this war, then I have to do this."

After escaping Russian occupation, Terekh began looking for a way to help. In the fall of 2022, Russia started attacking Ukrainian cities with Iranian-made, long-range Shahed exploding drones. It also started manufacturing its own versions, known as Gerans.

Terekh and Ukrainian businessman Denys Shtilerman, whom she had worked with designing outdoor urban spaces before the war, decided to build their own long-range attack drones to help Ukraine strike back.

Shtilerman had a background in defense engineering, but most other initial members of the team, including Terekh, came from civilian backgrounds. Yehor Skalyha, their third co-founder, was a film producer.

At first, the company aimed to build 20 of its FP-1 drones per month. By 2024, they were regularly being used to strike Russian airfields, ammunition depots and oil refineries. But over the last two years, the company's ambitions, and its arsenal, have grown.

Fire Point now makes 300 to 400 long-range attack drones per day, and it has added more advanced weapons to its production lines.

In June, a Fire Point cruise missile completed a mission of over 1,000 miles, which she claimed as the longest-range strike ever carried out by a cruise missile in combat history.

Terekh also made the bold claim that Ukraine has launched twice as many deep strikes into Russia as Russia has into Ukraine in 2026 — with 60% of the Ukrainian attacks using Fire Point weapons.

She said her company is now just months away from deploying Ukraine's first domestically designed and manufactured ballistic missile. Unlike cruise missiles, which stay lower to the ground, ballistic missiles follow an arc trajectory that takes them much higher, making them harder to intercept.

Fire Point is among many Ukrainian startups that have helped to shift the country from being solely a recipient of military aid to an engine of defense technology innovation.

Many other companies have similar, unlikely stories of their beginnings. The founder of Sine Engineering, which has attracted American investment in its communications and navigation technology, ran a business making standing desks before the war. Yaroslav Azhnyuk, founder of the Fourth Law, which makes autonomous guidance systems for drones, previously founded Petcube, a pet tech startup backed by the American business accelerator Y Combinator.

Terekh believes these companies, with their founders' diverse backgrounds outside the defense sector and their shared ability to pivot to new endeavors, have been key to their successes.

"This works in Ukraine because we have very low bureaucracy, because we have direct communication with the army, and because we have companies that react," she said.

The country's innovative approach to defense manufacturing and procurement has also attracted the attention of its allies.

In 2025, the U.S. military announced its own program to copy Iran's Shahed drones, known as "LUCAS," which deployed its first relatively cheap long-range drones in the Middle East in February.

The U.S. and Ukrainian governments are expected to sign a new defense agreement soon that would expand Ukrainian military technology exports to the U.S. and joint ventures with American companies.

Terekh said Fire Point's primary focus remains on Ukraine's defense, but she welcomed the idea of one day playing a role in a new, wider Western security architecture.

"We need to ensure that Ukraine will stop just being a breadbasket for the world," she said, referring to the country's longtime primary export of grains. "Now we have something to offer which is much more valuable, and the defense industry is a huge driver for this."

title: Eiffel Tower closed due to strike after female staff allegedly removed for religious group
description: The Eiffel Tower in Paris was closed on Monday as employees went on strike to protest claims female colleagues were told to stay out of sight during a visit by a Hindu religious group, drawing critici...
fullText:
The Eiffel Tower in Paris was closed on Monday as employees went on strike to protest claims female colleagues were told to stay out of sight during a visit by a Hindu religious group, drawing criticism from French politicians.

Around 100 members of the Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha (BAPS), a global Hindu organization headquartered in Ahmedabad, India, visited the landmark on Saturday.

BAPS describes itself as a "spiritual, volunteer-driven fellowship" dedicated to improving society through individual growth and promoting the Hindu values of faith, service and global harmony. The group inaugurated a new Hindu temple in Paris on Sunday.

Diane Davoine, a union representative for the Eiffel Tower staff, told reporters that during the visit, "women were asked to leave their places of work in order to place men there."

"So that absolutely does not go down well with the employees, with women obviously, who are all humiliated by what happened, by the way some were treated," she said.

Paris Mayor Emmanuel Grégoire said an investigation has been launched into the claims.

"It is not acceptable that such conditions can be tolerated," he wrote on X. "These are neither my values, nor those that the Eiffel Tower should uphold, where everyone should be able to move about and act freely, without distinction between women and men."

The Eiffel Tower Operating Company (SETE) acknowledged that the delegation had requested a visit that limited "interactions with women," according to CNN affiliate BFMTV.

SETE said that "these conditions should not have been accepted," BFMTV reported.

CNN has contacted SETE for a response.

In a statement on X, BAPS did not directly mention the female staff but said it took the concerns "very seriously" and that the visit was organized "in coordination with the Eiffel Tower team at the start of normal opening hours" to limit disruption to other visitors.

"To the best of our knowledge, at no point was anyone prevented access to the Eiffel Tower," the statement said. "Nevertheless, we sincerely apologise for any pain or inconvenience caused."

When reached by CNN for comment, BAPS Paris said in a statement, "It was never, at any point, intended as a request rooted in gender, and any suggestion to the contrary does not reflect the spirit or values of our fellowship or the delegation."

"BAPS remains firmly committed to the principles of equality, mutual respect, and service to all, regardless of gender, background, or belief – values that lie at the very heart of our tradition's teachings and community work worldwide," the statement continued.

News of the closure made headlines in India on Tuesday. Some commentators on social media asked why the monument's management complied with the purported request to sideline female staff. Several others said the incident has stained India's credibility and the Hindu religion.

The incident has sparked outrage in a country with a long history of feminist activism and a constitutional commitment to secularism that traces its ideological origins to the French Revolution.

Over the past century, feminist movements in France have also successfully pioneered campaigns for women's suffrage, reproductive rights and greater gender equality. France became the first country in the world to guarantee the right to abortion in its constitution in 2024.

France's Minister for Gender Equality and the Fight Against Discrimination, Aurore Bergé, called the alleged incident at the Eiffel Tower "unacceptable."

"In France, gender equality is neither negotiable nor subject to varying standards. It is a principle, and there are no exceptions to it," she wrote on X.

Thousands of Hindu devotees associated with BAPS joined various events and processions in France in recent days, according to its website.

Last week, a procession "led by women and girls of all ages" made its way down the streets of Bussy-Saint-Georges, an eastern suburb in the French capital, according to BAPS. More than 5,500 Hindu devotees from around the world also joined a boat procession on the River Seine, it said.

BAPS is known for its ornate temples across the world.

The BAPS Swaminarayan Akshardham in Robbinsville, New Jersey, is the largest Hindu temple in the United States. It also built the largest Hindu temple in the United Arab Emirates, which Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi inaugurated in 2024.

Hinduism is widely considered to be the world's oldest living religion and the third largest – behind Christianity and Islam – with more than 1 billion followers.

Among other things, Hinduism reveres femininity through the worship of powerful goddesses, including Saraswati, the goddess of wisdom; Kali, the goddess who destroys evil and ego; and Lakshmi, the goddess of wealth and prosperity.

Yet entrenched misogyny and debates over gender equality within the religion have persisted, particularly over women's access to temples and certain rituals.

In a landmark 2018 ruling, India's Supreme Court struck down a centuries-old ban on women of menstrual age entering the Sabarimala Temple in the southern state of Keralam, declaring the restriction discriminatory and unconstitutional.

title: NYC releases trove of 9/11 documents showing officials knew air quality at Ground Zero was unsafe
description: The release of more than 170,000 pages of records comes days before the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001, terror attacks.
fullText:
New York City on Tuesday released more than 170,000 pages of records showing that officials knew the air quality around Ground Zero following the Sept. 11, 2001, terror attacks was unsafe despite repeatedly assuring residents and first responders the air was safe to breathe.

The documents — including previously unreleased air quality reports, contamination records and memos between officials — were posted online by New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani's office days ahead of the 25th anniversary of the attacks.

"On Friday, we will mark 25 years since the worst tragedy to ever befall our city, the darkest day New York City has ever known," Mamdani said at a news conference surrounded by 9/11 survivors and families. "And yet, the devastating truth is that the suffering did not end once the smoke cleared and the dust settled. For so many New Yorkers who lived or worked or studied near Ground Zero, and for the thousands of others who worked on the pile, recovering those we lost and clearing the rubble, that was only the beginning."

Nearly 3,000 people were killed in the attacks. But according to Mamdani, more people have died from 9/11-related illnesses than were killed on the day itself.

"People got sick because the leaders they trusted lied and told them they were safe to breathe in toxic air," Mamdani said.

The mayor was joined by Jon Stewart, host of The Daily Show and a longtime advocate for first responders and people with 9/11-related illnesses.

"There was poison in the air, and on the ground, and in the windowsills, and in your air conditioners and covering your pets and your clothes, and it stayed there for months," Stewart said. "Everyone knew. Now it's very clear that the city knew as well."

The records, which had been stored in 68 boxes in a city office, were discovered last year, according to the mayor's office, and posted to a searchable online database. They include the so-called Harding memo, sent to then-Mayor Rudy Giuliani's deputy mayor, Robert Harding, in which officials discussed ways to limit the city's liability for toxic exposure.

Their release follows the settlement of a pair of lawsuits brought by 9/11 Health Watch, which had sued to force their publication. More documents are expected to be posted to the portal in the coming months.

"The very least our city owes the families, survivors and first responders whose lives were forever changed by the September 11th attacks is transparency and accountability," Mamdani said in a statement. "For too long, New Yorkers have had to fight for access to records that should have been available to them in the first place."

Mamdani is scheduled to attend more than a half-dozen events this week marking the 25th anniversary of 9/11.

In an appearance on Newsmax over the weekend, Giuliani said Mamdani's decision to attend them "offends" him, repeating baseless and Islamophobic claims about the city's first Muslim mayor and comparing him with the 9/11 terrorists.

Mamdani declined to respond directly when asked about Giuliani's comments on Monday.

"I'm proud to be the mayor of this city. I love this city. I love this country," Mamdani said. "And what I want this week to be a focus on is the families whose loved ones were stolen from them 25 years ago in the horrific act of terror of Sept. 11, and a focus also on the first responders who did everything they could for this city."

title: Subject: Untitled
description: Ahmed...
fullText:
Poems

 / 
 September 8, 2026

Subject: Untitled

 Ahmed Shamali 

Everything in Gaza is crucified on the edge of loss: the air is broken, the sky is perforated, and mothers give birth to silence that has neither beginning nor end. Nothing here is born whole, even the stories come out truncated. And laughter, when it happens, seems strange, as if trying to escape madness and failing every time. The remains of the houses speak for themselves, telling tales of death and survival, whispering what has not been heard, and what will never be heard. Every window beneath the rubble preserves the image of an explosion, and every corner remembers those who left and never returned. The birds are silent, as if the sky itself is afraid to tell us what is to come. We fear the light as we fear the darkness. We fear falling asleep lest the dream be obliterated, and we fear waking to find our hearts have changed their address. The night is long, hope is short, and survival is postponed until further notice. Schools are empty of children, yet the echo of their voices reverberates through the demolished alleys. Gaza is a city that, whenever it buries its children, gives birth to new patience. It experiences death for the thousandth time and does not die. It rises as if redefining the miracle every day. We are not okay, my friends.

title: Angie Nixon Is Fighting for the Right to Read
description: Katrina vanden Heuvel, John Nichols, The...
fullText:
The Florida Senate candidate responded to Republican book-banning schemes by opening a bookstore.

For many years, Angie Nixon has led the charge against the nefarious schemes of Florida Republicans to ban books that present an unfiltered history of the United States. This fight is just a part of what makes the Democratic state legislator an inspiring candidate for the US Senate. But it strikes us as a qualification that deserves special note at a time when the right to read is under attack. As we publish The Nation’s Fall Books issue, we’re thinking a lot about the role that books play in opening up this country’s discourse.

We value texts that reflect on the injustices of the past and the present—and that amplify activism to remedy those injustices. But there are plenty of right-wing politicians who see a threat in books that provide a full picture of the struggle for a more perfect union.

Florida has in recent years been ground zero in the battle over the freedom to read. And Angie Nixon has bravely stood on the right side of history. Long before she won a surprise victory in the Florida Democratic Senate primary on August 19—and, because of her progressive positions and membership in the Democratic Socialists of America, suddenly became a national figure—Nixon started a bookstore in her hometown of Jacksonville that puts banned books front and center on the shelves. In so doing, she offered a contemporary expression of what Frederick Douglass described as “a sublime faith in the great principles of justice and freedom” that has always animated the greatest of American activists and leaders. The story of her bookstore, Café Resistance, is one of courage and words-into-deeds action, and it gets to the heart of how Democrats should position themselves in the so-called culture wars that Republicans always gin up at election time. Instead of cowering, Democrats should take a cue from Nixon’s inspired efforts to embrace and celebrate historically marginalized and oppressed peoples.

Nixon stepped up four years ago, when Florida Governor Ron DeSantis was laying the groundwork for his failed 2024 presidential campaign with initiatives designed to position him as his party’s most ardent critic of diversity, equity, and inclusion. The Florida branch of the ACLU complained that DeSantis “sought to censor Black history in classrooms and called slavery ‘beneficial’ for Black people.” The governor’s assault on the truth included advocacy for legislation that empowered local book-banning schemes and what PEN America Florida has described as “rampant free expression infringements in Florida.” These “speech-constricting laws, policies, and book bans,” PEN argues, advance an agenda with “very real consequences for students, educators, and the freedom to read in this state” and “have become a template for conservative activists and lawmakers behind the movement that has led to nearly 6,000 instances of book bans since 2021.”

Nixon offered an alternative template that defended, as she puts it, “the freedom for our children to learn true history and not have books banned for political purposes.” She was an outspoken foe of the book-banning legislation on the floor of the state House of Representatives, to which she was elected in 2020. And when the Republican majority rejected her arguments, Nixon started the bookstore and community hub. “In 2022, Governor Ron DeSantis signed House Bill 1467, and Florida became the state with the most book bans in the country,” she says. “So I stocked the books they tried to pull off the shelves. And Café Resistance was born. They banned the truth, so we put it right here in the community: free tutoring, coffee, and the books they don’t want kids to read.”

That’s what the owners of independent bookstores do in urban neighborhoods and small cities and towns all over the country. They make their shops havens not merely for books and their authors (including Nixon, who has cowritten a children’s book with her daughter) but also for young readers, many of whom find a sense of possibility in books by and about Harriet Tubman, Rosa Parks, Shirley Chisholm, Angela Davis, and the 1619 Project. The same goes for public libraries and school libraries, where so many librarians have bravely stood up to the red-state politicians who attack the right to read—and the honest discourse that extends from that reading.

We imagine a good many shop clerks and librarians will be cheering Angie Nixon on, because the US Senate has enough establishment politicians. It could use a bookstore owner.

title: Trump told Putin he wants swift end to Ukraine war and US-Russia ties restored - Kremlin

fullText:
MOSCOW, Sept 8 (Reuters) - U.S. President Donald Trump told Russian President Vladimir Putin on Tuesday in a phone call that ‌he wanted a swift end to the war in Ukraine, ‌something that would allow U.S.-Russia ties to be fully restored, the Kremlin said.

Kremlin aide ​Yuri Ushakov told reporters that the pair had discussed the outcome of U.S. peace negotiators' weekend visit to Moscow and Kyiv - something he said both leaders had rated "with a plus sign" - and said that Putin had ‌told Trump what he ⁠believed the United States could do to help end the conflict.

Putin had also given Trump his assessment of what ⁠the situation on the battlefield was and had made it clear that Russia had no hostile plans towards Europe, Ushakov said.

"Donald Trump clearly emphasised the ​desirability of ​bringing the conflict to an ​end as soon as possible, ‌which would immediately open up prospects – impressive and far-reaching ones at that – for the full restoration of relations between the U.S. and Russia," said Ushakov.

"In his view, this would have a particular impact on trade and economic ties, promising enormous benefits for both countries. Donald Trump ‌is keen to see a breakthrough ​achieved during his presidency. Vladimir Vladimirovich Putin ​supported this approach".

Ushakov - who said ​Putin and Trump had also agreed on the ‌need to continue prisoner exchanges - said he ​was not able ​to get into more details about what had been discussed, but described the conversation as constructive and said the two leaders had ​agreed they would stay ‌in touch and speak to each other by phone again ​if the needed arose.

Unearthed interview exposes what Talarico thought about 'tough-on-crime' tactics
description: Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico pushed restorative justice over suspension and expulsion, linking school discipline to criminal reform.
fullText:
James Talarico, the Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate in Texas, once framed disciplinary practices in schools as an outflow of the ideas behind criminal justice reforms he hoped lawmakers would implement in Texas.

"I'm recently excited about the formation of a bipartisan criminal justice reform caucus in the Texas House with prominent Democrats and prominent Republicans who understand that we have to move away from a tough-on-crime approach to a smart-on-crime approach, and that, I think, filters down to our schools," Talarico said in a 2020 interview on school disciplinary practices and their effect on minorities.

Talarico's train of thought, from criminal reform laws to changes in educational discipline, demonstrates his underlying beliefs about moving away from punitive corrections.

Soros Network Rebuilds Progressive Prosecutor Push After String Of Election Losses

Talarico fleshed out his view, detailing how the changes would affect the educational system.

"[We are] starting in elementary school, where we really pursue restorative practices that are going to rehabilitate our students who are suffering from trauma, our students who are feeling unsafe in school and our students who harm a classroom community."

Talarico was referring to "restorative justice," a view that links misbehavior to past personal and emotional experiences. In the words of Texas Appleseed, a group that promotes "social, economic and racial justice," restorative justice in education emphasizes the relational cost of conflict as a way to deter future bad behavior. "Restorative Justice, when applied to a school setting, focuses on how student behavior has harmed others and how to make amends. Schools use it to build community and strengthen student–school connections," the group wrote in a definition submitted to lawmakers.

The approach is often mentioned as an alternative to "zero tolerance" policies that focus on punishments that deter discouraged conduct.

To Talarico, its adoption could deemphasize other forms of punishments.

"What that means is really allowing students to repair the harms that they've caused in a classroom community. It's a lot more rigorous and a lot more effective than just expelling a student or suspending a student or removing them from a classroom community," Talarico said.

While in the Texas legislature in 2021, Talarico introduced a bill, HB 62, which would have sought to move schools away from in-school suspension, out-of-school suspension and removing kids to alternative educational programs.

The bill stalled in committee and never became law.

North Carolina Teacher's Killing Reignites Scrutiny Of Roy Cooper's Criminal Justice Record In Senate Race

In the wake of the Uvalde school shooting in 2022, Republican lawmakers pushed back against Talarico's line of reasoning, arguing that, despite some calls for leniency, repercussions for problematic behavior are sometimes unavoidable.

"Look, I don't want to see a kid go to jail for being caught with some pot. I don't want to see a kid go to jail because he gets into a fight with another kid," Texas state Rep. Steve Toth, a Republican, told interviewers.

"That's clearly not the intent here. But if you've got a kid that is violent and is consistently violent, and they've been violent toward other children and teachers, then we either have to reach that kid or we have to remove that kid. They shouldn't be in the classroom. Period."

Talarico's statements are consistent with past calls to step away from law enforcement and prisons and towards social programs — calls that also show his beliefs about the best ways to deter criminal behavior.

"If we took just half of what we spent on wars, prisons, and policing and spent it on education, health care, and jobs, we could make prisons obsolete," Talarico said in a 2022 speech to a graduation ceremony for incarcerated students.

A little later on in that same speech, Talarico went further, calling the idea of prisons themselves a kind of violence.

"My experience as a teacher, a legislator, and a Christian tells me that birds don't belong in cages; children don't belong in cages; people don't belong in cages. Poverty is violence. Pollution is violence. And yes, prison is violence," Talarico said.

Michigan Senate Hopeful Abdul El-sayed Fires Back At Cnn Choosing To 'Fixate' On 'Defund The Police' Comments

"I'm not asking you to join the system; I'm asking you to change the system. Dismantle this system of violence."

When asked about his views on criminal justice and how they link to education, Talarico's campaign said he has always prioritized both safety and smart-on-crime approaches, noting that he had been a member of the state's criminal reform caucus.

"James joined his Republican colleagues on this caucus because as a former public school teacher, James cares about keeping Texas students safe. James agrees with most Texans that we government should be smart-on-crime, and our students deserve all the support possible," JT Ennis, a campaign spokesperson, said in a statement to Fox News Digital.

"While James has passed bills in the legislature to deny bail for violent criminals, crack down on violent felons and send billions of dollars to support law enforcement, Ken Paxton has abused his office to benefit his wealthy donors and the well-connected — allowing criminals back on the street even as it made Texans less safe. Even Ken Paxton's fellow Republicans have blasted his public safety record: more murders, soft on human trafficking, and pedophiles walking free," he added, referring to Talarico's Republican challenger, former Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton.

Having cleared the primary and secured his party's nomination, Talarico will face off against Paxton in the Nov. 3 general election.

Witness says pilot in Amazon crash was shaking afterward: "My career is over"
description: Abraham Altamar was on the phone with his wife when he briefly spoke with one of the pilots of the Amazon cargo plane that overran a runway in Miami.
fullText:
One of the pilots of an Amazon cargo plane that overshot a Miami runway and killed five people was shaking and in distress after emerging from the plane's cockpit, a witness told CBS News.

Abraham Altamar said the fiery crash at Miami International Airport was "surreal" and "scary" to witness. Altamar, who had been working at a nearby building, was on FaceTime with his wife when the pilot approached him.

"He was, like, shaking and, and a little injured in his forehead and his hand," Altamar said. "I was like, 'Hey, you want me to call 911?' He's like, 'No, we already called them.'"

The pilot then said he needed to call his wife, Altamar said. Altamar gave him his phone.

"He was just, like, telling her that he was fine, 'Just tell my mom that I was in the accident, but I'm already out of the plane, that I'm good,'" Altamar said. His wife, Alexis Altamar, noted that the pilot was upset and said, "My career is over."

The pilots were identified Tuesday as Joseph Carroll, 55, and Jaime Felipe Silva Molina, 37. It wasn't immediately clear which pilot Altamar spoke with. Both pilots were treated for injuries and have been released, National Transportation Safety Board Chair Jennifer Homendy said.

CBS News has determined the names of the pilots using a Miami-Dade Sheriff's Office news release, LinkedIn profiles, and the Federal Aviation Administration's pilot database. LinkedIn profiles list Carroll as a captain with 21 Air, the carrier that operated the flight, and Silva as a 21 Air first officer.

The NTSB is investigating the incident. Investigators arrived on the scene Monday. Officials say the plane struck navigation equipment before hitting a cleaning crew van with seven people inside. The plane then went through a fence, struck a Toyota SUV driving outside the airport, and barreled through another fence before coming to a stop near a fleet of parked Tesla robotaxis.

All five of those killed were in the two struck vehicles.

New cellphone video appears to show one crew member jumping out of the plane after the crash. The NTSB has yet to interview the pilot and co-pilot of the plane. The plane's two black boxes, which record voice and flight data, have been recovered and sent to the NTSB's headquarters in Washington, D.C., for analysis. Aircraft operator 21 Air and Amazon say they are cooperating fully with the investigation.

Homendy described the crash scene as "devastating."

"You can see, on the paved surface, tire marks that continues through the grass," Homendy said in a news conference Monday. "There's debris everywhere."

Officials said that part of their investigation will look into whether installing a safety bed at the end of a runway to help stop a plane should be more common at airports nationwide. The safety feature, known as an Engineered Materials Arresting System, or EMAS, is used at more than 70 airports, according to the FAA. It is made of light, crushable material that allows an aircraft's tires to sink in, slowing the plane down and bringing it to a safe stop if it overruns the runway.

EMAS is generally used at airports that do not have a full 1,000-foot safety area at the end of a runway. The runway that the plane overran does have that 1,000-foot safety area, Miami International Airport told CBS Miami.

title: IRS under Trump unlawfully shared taxpayer info with immigration authorities, court rules
description: A U.S. appeals court on Tuesday upheld an injunction blocking an Internal Revenue Service policy that allowed it to share thousands of taxpayers' addresses with
fullText:
Sept 8 (Reuters) - A U.S. appeals court on Tuesday upheld an injunction blocking an Internal Revenue Service policy that allowed it to share thousands of taxpayers' ‌addresses with immigration authorities, saying the Trump administration's practice violated federal law.

A three-judge panel of ‌the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit ruled that the IRS last year disclosed roughly 47,000 ​taxpayer addresses to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement under a procedure adopted as part of the administration's efforts to expand immigration enforcement.

The IRS and U.S. Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, did not respond to requests for comment.

Under an agreement between the agencies, the IRS in July 2025 began processing ICE ‌requests for the last known addresses ⁠of as many as 1.28 million people suspected of unlawfully residing in the United States.

The IRS adopted a procedure that allowed ICE to obtain information on ⁠taxpayers if it provided a five- or nine-digit number in an address field, even if that number was not an actual ZIP code.

Groups including the Center for Taxpayer Rights and the Main Street Alliance sued, arguing ​the ​practice was unlawful. A lower-court judge agreed and blocked ​the policy, by which time the IRS ‌had already shared 47,289 records with ICE.

President Donald Trump's administration on appeal contended the ruling hindered federal law enforcement.

"But that's a gripe with Congress, not the court," U.S. Circuit Judge Cornelia Pillard said in the appeals court's ruling.

Pillard, like the rest of the three-judge panel, was appointed by Democratic President Barack Obama.

After the Watergate scandal during President Richard Nixon's era exposed abuses of U.S. taxpayers' information, Congress barred ‌the IRS sharing information with other government agencies unless ​they complied with stringent conditions.

Pillard said the procedures the IRS ​under Trump adopted violated federal law in ​numerous ways, including "most egregiously" by not even requiring ICE to provide an actual ‌address for a taxpayer as legally required.

The ​practice, Pillard said, "automates the review ​of millions of records without any individual review or any other means of ensuring compliance with the legal prerequisites to releasing each individual taxpayer's information."

Skye Perryman, whose liberal legal group ​Democracy Forward represented the plaintiffs, ‌in a statement said she was pleased the court "acted to stop this unlawful behavior."

"The privacy ​laws enacted in the post-Watergate era exist to prevent abuses of power just like ​this," she said.

title: Bears Rookie Gets Thrown Into the Fire in Week 1
description: Dillon Thieneman dreamed about his first NFL regular-season game as a kid. Now, the Chicago Bears rookie safety will get […]
fullText:
Dillon Thieneman dreamed about his first NFL regular-season game as a kid. Now, the Chicago Bears rookie safety will get there with far more on his shoulders than most first-year players could expect.

The Bears open their 2026 season Sunday against the Carolina Panthers needing Thieneman to be more than a promising young player. They need him to be steady. They need him to communicate. And, most of all, they need him to help eliminate the backbreaking explosive plays that undermined their defense in recent years.

That is a massive assignment for any rookie, particularly one walking into an unsettled safety room.

Chicago lost projected starter Coby Bryant to a major knee injury during training camp, and the team placed slot cornerback Kyler Gordon on the physically unable-to-perform list. Gordon must miss at least the first four games, potentially more. The Bears have veteran options in Xavier Woods and Cam Lewis alongside Thieneman, but neither uncertainty disappears simply because the regular season is here.

Thieneman, the rookie selected 25th overall in April, has become the constant.

That is not how the Bears envisioned their back end at the start of camp. But Thieneman handled the summer well enough that the team can reasonably expect him to play a major role immediately. His range, instinctiveness and willingness to tackle have shown up throughout camp and the preseason. His next challenge is preventing the mistakes that turn a good defensive call into a 40-yard gain.

Dillon Thieneman showing off the range to breakup this pass intended for Carnell Tate

Future perennial Pro Bowler pic.twitter.com/AFQ6eJrwaJ

Chicago's defense struggled to limit explosive plays last season, a weakness that puts more pressure on its reshaped safety group. That is not a problem one player can solve alone, but safeties are often the final line of defense when a coverage breaks down or a runner gets through the first two levels.

Thieneman knows the difference between merely understanding the system and playing quickly within it.

"I've got a better understanding of tendencies," he said Monday. "So now it's taking that next step and not only just knowing it, but being able to anticipate it and use it to your advantage."

That is the leap the Bears need him to make sooner rather than later.

Defensive coordinator Dennis Allen's scheme should help. Thieneman said the defense has structure and rules, but Allen does not want defenders frozen by the call sheet. He gives players room to communicate, adjust and trust what they see before the snap.

"I think it's pretty simple," Thieneman said. "Obviously, there's complexities within it, but a lot of times he makes a call and he lets people on the field just play football. … If we see it a little differently, he's like, 'You guys are out on the field. You guys call it.' That's been pretty cool."

That freedom is valuable, but it also demands maturity. A rookie safety can get himself into trouble by trying to make the perfect play rather than the correct one. Thieneman will have to balance his aggressive instincts with the discipline to stay on top of routes, make the proper checks and ensure everyone in the secondary sees the formation the same way.

The Bears did not leave him alone to figure that out. Thieneman has spent camp working alongside Lewis and Woods, two veterans with far more NFL experience. He said he feels comfortable with both players and regularly talks through what they saw on the field and the sideline.

"They definitely have a lot of experience able to help me," Thieneman said. "I've been talking to them a lot just in the meeting room, like how they see things. And out on the field, we'll talk once we're on the sideline. But I feel very comfortable and able to communicate and kind of anticipate what the other guys are thinking."

That comfort matters because Chicago could need all three players in different roles. Lewis has experience at safety and nickel cornerback. Woods brings physicality and has pushed for a starting job since signing late in camp. Rookie Malik Muhammad appears positioned to begin in the slot while Gordon is sidelined, but the Bears have options if they decide they need Lewis there instead.

The lineup may change. Thieneman's importance will not.

He has already received practical advice on handling the inevitable ups and downs of a rookie season. Assistant defensive backs coach Matt Giordano told him to learn from the bad moments without letting them linger.

"Just take it one day at a time," Thieneman said. "Something bad happens, learn from it, move on. Don't linger too long."

That philosophy will get tested quickly. The Panthers will look for every communication lapse and every inexperienced defender they can isolate. The Bears cannot bet on their rookie safety to be perfect in Week 1, but they need him to be poised.

Thieneman has waited a long time for this moment. The Bears are asking him to make the most of it immediately.

fullText:
Shaquille O'Neal receives a brutal response from Jemele Hill over Stephen A. Smith's defense.

NBA analyst Stephen A. Smith, Jemele Hill, and Cari Champion continue to make headlines after the ESPN icon's alleged three-hour interview with them.

Smith has alleged that Hill and Champion edited clips out of the interview to make him look bad rather than clearing the air about his 2014 comments.

Now, NBA legend Shaquille O'Neal has joined the conversation, but the former LA Lakers superstar received a brutal response from Hill.

All O'Neal did was repost Smith's demand that Hill and Champion release the full footage of the interview. But Hill interpreted it as feeding into the false narrative.

As a result, Hill posted a lengthy response to the Diesel on X, stating, "I hate to even address this because it's feeding a false narrative.

"The full interview is out on iHeart, Apple Podcasts, or wherever you get your podcasts and has been that way from the beginning. An editing mistake occurred involving the video, and no, Cari and I don't have anything to do with the video, and that is why there is some video footage unaccounted for."

Hill added, "This mistake was shared with Stephen A's team, and they were also provided a full transcript as well as told exactly how it happened. Nothing nefarious occurred.

"Trust me, there is no smoking gun in the unseen video footage, and you can go to the audio and listen for yourselves. The 20 minutes that is alleged to be missing is all there in the audio version."

Hill blamed the mistake on the editing team as she put Smith's claims to bed. But will it be enough to calm the ESPN analyst and, more importantly, Shaq? Only time will tell.

title: Wycombe sack boss Duff after winless start
description: Wycombe Wanderers sack Michael Duff and his assistant Alex Morris just five games into the League One season.
fullText:
Wycombe Wanderers have sacked Michael Duff as manager following a five-game winless start to the new League One season.

First-team coach Alex Morris has also left the club in the wake of the Buckinghamshire side having picked up just three points out of a possible 15.

The 48-year-old former Cheltenham Town, Barnsley, Swansea City and Huddersfield boss had been in charge almost a year after replacing Michael Dodds on 18 September 2025, having made a similarly poor start to last season.

Wycombe recovered to finish in the top half of the table and although they have only actually lost twice this time round in the league, it has not stopped Duff becoming the first managerial casualty of the campaign in the top four divisions.

"The appointment of an interim head coach will follow later today," said a club statement.

"The club has made the decision in light of a disappointing run of results since the spring and believes the time is right to take a new direction."

Although they beat Rotherham on the final day of last season, that has been Wycombe's sole victory in their past 13 games, in all competitions, including this season's Carabao Cup defeat by Stevenage and the Vertu Trophy draw at Reading.

Former Crewe Alexandra manager Morris had been with Wycombe since October 2025, after spending two years on the coaching staff at Stoke City.
